references.text: Jesus had just called his first disciples ([ref:Joh 1:35-51|John 1:35-51]), and it is these disciples who now follow him to the wedding in Cana.

Jesus gladly participated in social gatherings and meals. In [ref:Matt 9:10|Matthew 9:10], Jesus sits at the table with tax collectors and sinners, showing that he did not isolate himself but was present among people in their daily lives.

Jesus' participation in social gatherings such as weddings led his opponents to call him "a glutton and a drunkard" ([ref:Luk 7:34|Luke 7:34]). This shows that Jesus lived close to people and was not ascetic like John the Baptist.
The parallel passage in [ref:Matt 11:19|Matthew 11:19] emphasizes the same point: The Son of Man came and both ate and drank, unlike John the Baptist.

That Jesus participated in the wedding shows his true humanity. He had to become like his brothers in every way ([ref:Hebr 2:17|Hebrews 2:17]), and fully took part in human life, including festive occasions.
The wedding in Cana where Jesus and his disciples were invited became the place of Jesus' first sign, where he revealed his glory and his disciples came to believe in him ([ref:Joh 2:11|John 2:11]).

The wedding motif recurs throughout the Bible. In [ref:Åp 19:9|Revelation 19:9] it is said: "Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb." Jesus as a guest at the wedding in Cana points forward to the eschatological marriage feast.

In Jesus' parable about the king's son's wedding ([ref:Matt 22:2-3|Matthew 22:2-3]), the wedding invitation is used as an image of God's call to people. Jesus' own participation in a wedding provides a concrete background for the wedding motif in his preaching.
